text: For the "Harvard Dad," planning for Harvard was merely an outcome, not the ultimate objective; what mattered most to him was whether his child possessed the capacity for independent thought. His core philosophy can be distilled into two key concepts: "meticulous design" and "meticulous free-range nurturing."
A peaceful park right by the river with lovely, nature themed granite bollards and ground plates by artist William Reimann.
Love this park in honor of my Aunt!
Another beautiful Oasis in a dense metro neighborhood. Creates a needed break to the brick and pavement giving families and all a peace with calm pause.

We were lucky enough to have our wedding reception at State Park and truly could not have imagined a better experience. Chelsea was incredible to work with. She always available to answer our questions, and so helpful in planning the flow of the night. She made the entire process feel easy and stress-free.

The night of the wedding, Nicholas managed everything seamlessly and kept the evening running so smoothly behind the scenes so we could actually relax and enjoy ourselves. The bartenders absolutely crushed it. Every drink was amazing and they somehow kept the bar moving incredibly fast all night long.

Every single guest commented on how amazing the food was and how much fun they had. We’re still hearing about it weeks later. State Park created the perfect atmosphere for our reception and exceeded every expectation we had. We are so grateful to the entire team for making our wedding night feel so special. Highly, highly recommend!
Very unpleasant experience with the attendant who was unaware of 10 reserved parking spaces for a memorial service at the chapel.

The place is so comfortable and welcoming! The staff are really kind and always ready to help with everything. My experience was amazing — I truly enjoyed it and learned a lot from the course with Miss Nicholas. I’d definitely love to do it again! 💛✨

Do residents of Cambridge vote for the stuff forced upon you? Number one, please read the drawbacks to the place based treaty. They are real…but if your constituents want it, then far be it from me to complain. Also, I can’t imagine riding a bike home from work after being on my feet from 6am to 5pm. Are any of the commuting bike riders blue collar? I’m not from your area so moving here was a shock. Are the bike lanes something that a majority of the people in your town want or was it forced upon them? I avoid your city while staying in Belmont (wild how far I’m willing to drive around to avoid) because it’s a standstill with no lanes. (Except for Phil’s awesome twenty dollar haircuts. I’ll always deal with traffic for his place) Do you want your city to have no conservative or poor ppl living there? That seems like a recipe for failure of a tax base in such a dense area

This is a great place to stop and wander around to see the art pieces.  No entry fee, they have a kids scavenger hunt which made it interesting for my kid to go through every floor and look at everything. The AC made it better on a hot day where you can sit and admire the paintings too.

I just ate there and, it was a very disappointing meal.  The soup came out cold and steak tip were ice cold.  The waitress never came back to check on us , so I got up to speak host and he never sent over the waitress.  Finally we had to flag her down .  They took the two items off our bill but the manger never came over till I asked for him.
A very disappointing experience .

Kresge Auditorium reminds me of a wedge of an egg. The interior and exterior are beautiful.  The acoustics are clear inside the auditorium.  There is a whispering gallery.  You can go to one end inside and whisper and a person at the other end of the gallery can hear you distinctly.  There is no other building that looks like Kresge.  You can sit or lie on the base of the building outside or try to climb it -- you won't get far.  One of the great mysteries is the lack of elevators or accessibility for people with physical limitations.  The restrooms are in the basement which are around 18 steps and there is a lift for final three stairs, but why not put a lift for the other 15 steps?  Basically, for people with issues with steps, you need to climb stairs to get into the Auditorium, you need to walk down stairs for the Little Kresge Theatre, and the most steps are to the restrooms.  Eero Saarinen the architect was probably able-bodied and didn't think beyond aesthetics and acoustics.
